eras.title: A Yoruba kingdom
eras.text: Oyo is one of several Yoruba kingdoms in today's south-western Nigeria, looking to the holy city of Ife. It is driven from its capital by the Nupe in the 16th century and rebuilds.

eras.title: The Oyo Empire
eras.text: With a powerful cavalry, Oyo dominates the region from the Niger to Dahomey, which pays it tribute, and grows rich from trade with the coast, including the Atlantic slave trade. Civil war and the Sokoto jihad bring its collapse in the 1830s.

eras.title: The Golden Stool
eras.text: Osei Tutu and the priest Okomfo Anokye unite the Akan states around Kumasi. Asante grows rich on gold and on trade with European forts on the coast, and builds a sophisticated state with roads and a bureaucracy.

eras.title: Wars with Britain
eras.text: Asante fights a series of wars with Britain; Kumasi is burned in 1874, and after the War of the Golden Stool led by Queen Mother Yaa Asantewaa (1900) Asante is annexed to the Gold Coast colony.

eras.title: The Hausa city-states
eras.text: Walled city-states such as Kano, Katsina and Zazzau in northern Nigeria grow rich on trans-Saharan trade, cloth and leatherwork, often paying tribute to Songhai or Kanem-Bornu, until the Sokoto jihad overthrows their kings.

eras.title: The Sokoto Caliphate
eras.text: Founded by Usman dan Fodio's jihad, this federation of emirates is one of the largest and most populous states of 19th-century Africa, a centre of Islamic scholarship, until the British conquer it in 1903.

eras.title: The Mossi kingdoms
eras.text: Horse-riding Mossi kingdoms centred on Ouagadougou in today's Burkina Faso resist the Mali and Songhai empires and keep their traditional religion, until French conquest in 1896.

eras.title: Mutapa
eras.text: A Shona state that succeeds Great Zimbabwe, controlling gold mines and the trade to the Swahili coast. The Portuguese try to conquer it in the 16th–17th centuries and make it a vassal for a time.

eras.title: Ndongo and Queen Nzinga
eras.text: A Mbundu kingdom in today's Angola that fights the Portuguese colony of Luanda, a major source of the Atlantic slave trade. Queen Nzinga (ruled 1624–63) resists for four decades from her base in Matamba.

eras.title: The Luba and Lunda states
eras.text: In the savannas of the southern Congo basin, the Luba kingdom and its offshoot the Lunda empire build networks of tributary chiefdoms, trading copper, salt and later slaves and ivory with both African coasts.

eras.title: The Zulu Kingdom
eras.text: Shaka turns the Zulu into a military power that dominates south-east Africa. His successors face Boer settlers and the British, who are defeated at Isandlwana (1879) before conquering Zululand the same year.

eras.title: Dahomey
eras.text: A Fon kingdom in today's Benin, known for its all-female military regiments, which takes over the coastal slave ports in the 1720s. France conquers it in 1894.

eras.title: Buganda
eras.text: A centralised kingdom on the northern shore of Lake Victoria that expands in the 18th–19th centuries; its kabaka welcomes Arab traders and then Christian missionaries, before it becomes the core of the British Uganda Protectorate.

eras.title: The Sultanate of Sennar
eras.text: The Funj conquer the last Christian Nubian kingdom and rule the middle Nile from Sennar, until Muhammad Ali's Egyptian army conquers Sudan in 1821.

eras.title: Sultanate of Darfur
eras.text: The Keira dynasty rules Darfur in western Sudan, trading on the 'Forty Days Road' caravan route to Egypt, until it is absorbed into Anglo-Egyptian Sudan.

eras.title: The Adal Sultanate
eras.text: A Muslim state based at Harar in the Horn of Africa. Under Imam Ahmad 'Gragn' (1529–43), with Ottoman muskets, it nearly conquers Christian Ethiopia, which survives with Portuguese help.

eras.title: The Merina Kingdom
eras.text: Madagascar was settled by Austronesian seafarers from Borneo and by Africans. The highland Merina kingdom unifies most of the island in the 19th century under Radama I and Queen Ranavalona, until France annexes it in 1897.

eras.title: An Indian Ocean empire
eras.text: Omanis drive the Portuguese from Muscat (1650) and from the Swahili coast, building a maritime empire whose sultan moves his court to Zanzibar, centre of the clove and East African slave trades.

eras.title: Oman and Zanzibar
eras.text: The empire splits into the Sultanates of Oman and Zanzibar, both under British influence; Zanzibar joins Tanganyika to form Tanzania in 1964.

eras.title: The Malacca Sultanate
eras.text: Founded by the prince Parameswara, Malacca becomes the great entrepôt of Southeast Asia, where ships from India, Arabia, China and the islands meet, and spreads Islam through the Malay world. The Portuguese seize it in 1511.

eras.title: The Aceh Sultanate
eras.text: A powerful Muslim sultanate on northern Sumatra that trades pepper and fights the Portuguese in Malacca; it resists Dutch conquest in a war lasting from 1873 to 1904.

eras.title: Mataram in Java
eras.text: Hindu and Buddhist dynasties in Central and East Java build the temples of Borobudur and Prambanan.

eras.title: Toungoo Burma
eras.text: The Toungoo kings, above all Bayinnaung (1550–81), build briefly the largest empire in Southeast Asian history.

eras.title: The Konbaung dynasty
eras.text: A revived Burmese state sacks Ayutthaya (1767) but loses three wars to Britain, which annexes the whole country by 1885.

eras.title: Independent Myanmar
eras.text: Independent from 1948, Burma is ruled by the military for most of the time since 1962.

eras.title: Brunei
eras.text: A Muslim sultanate that once ruled much of Borneo and the southern Philippines; reduced to a small state by the 19th century, it is a British protectorate until 1984 and is now rich from oil.

eras.title: The Bengal Sultanate
eras.text: An independent sultanate in the rich, densely populated Ganges delta, exporting textiles and rice across the Indian Ocean, until it is absorbed by the Mughals.

eras.title: Nawabs of Bengal
eras.text: The Nawabs rule Mughal Bengal almost independently, until the East India Company's victory at Plassey (1757) makes Bengal the base of British power in India.

eras.title: The Sikh Empire
eras.text: Maharaja Ranjit Singh unites the Punjab from Lahore into a powerful, religiously tolerant state with a modern army; the British annex it after two Anglo-Sikh wars.

eras.title: The Rajput kingdoms
eras.text: Warrior clans rule kingdoms across north-western India from hill forts such as Chittor, resisting Turkic and Afghan invaders.

eras.title: Under the Mughals and the British
eras.text: Most Rajput rulers become allies and generals of the Mughals; under the British they remain princely states until India's independence.

eras.title: The Ghaznavids
eras.text: A Turkic dynasty ruling from Ghazni in Afghanistan; Mahmud of Ghazni raids deep into India and patronises the poet Ferdowsi and the scholar al-Biruni.

eras.title: The Samanids
eras.text: A Persian dynasty ruling Central Asia and eastern Iran from Bukhara, where New Persian literature is born and the young Avicenna studies in the royal library.

eras.title: Khwarazm
eras.text: A Turkic dynasty builds an empire from the Aral Sea to Iran, only to be destroyed by Genghis Khan after its shah executes Mongol envoys (1219–21).

eras.title: Qara Khitai
eras.text: Khitan refugees from northern China found a Chinese-style state in Central Asia ruling over Muslim subjects, until the Mongols absorb it.

eras.title: The Kazakh Khanate
eras.text: Nomadic clans break away from the Uzbeks to form the Kazakh Khanate on the steppe, later divided into three hordes that gradually fall under Russian rule.

eras.title: Kazakhstan
eras.text: After decades as a Soviet republic — site of the Baikonur cosmodrome and nuclear tests — Kazakhstan becomes independent in 1991.

eras.title: The Uzbek khanates
eras.text: After the Timurids, Uzbek dynasties rule the oasis cities of Bukhara, Khiva and later Kokand. Isolated as Silk Road trade declines, they become Russian protectorates in the 1860s–70s.

eras.title: Tiwanaku
eras.text: A great Andean civilisation centred near Lake Titicaca, with monumental stone gateways and raised-field farming, whose influence reaches across Bolivia, Peru and Chile.

eras.title: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy
eras.text: Five (from 1722, six) nations of the eastern Great Lakes united by the Great Law of Peace. A major power in the fur trade and in the wars between France and Britain, the confederacy splits during the American Revolution.

eras.title: Comanchería
eras.text: After adopting the horse, the Comanche dominate the southern Great Plains, raiding deep into Mexico and blocking Spanish expansion, until the US Army and the destruction of the bison herds force them onto a reservation.

eras.title: Hawaiian chiefdoms
eras.text: Polynesian settlers develop rival chiefdoms on each island, with intensive farming, fishponds and a strict kapu (taboo) system.

eras.title: The Hawaiian Kingdom
eras.text: Kamehameha I unites the islands; the kingdom modernises and is recognised internationally, until American sugar planters overthrow Queen Liliʻuokalani in 1893. The US annexes Hawaii in 1898.
